title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Definition/Introduction
content: Occupational therapy is sometimes confused with physical therapy; however, it is fundamentally an assessment and intervention approach that supports individuals through the therapeutic use of everyday activities. The process typically begins with an assessment, followed by a tailored intervention plan designed to help individuals maintain, recover, or develop meaningful activities or occupations. See Image. Occupational Therapy.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Definition/Introduction
content: This service is frequently provided in long-term care settings and is delivered by occupational therapists and occupational therapy assistants. An often overlooked component of occupational therapy is its focus on mental health and well-being, particularly important because many residents in long-term care facilities have a diagnosis of depression. [1] Interventions, whether individual or group, address the whole person to enhance physical, psychological, and social adaptation, ultimately supporting quality of life even in the presence of disability.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern
content: Occupations are the set of activities that are significant to the patient's cultural context, age-appropriate, chosen, organized, and carried out by each individual to provide for himself, to derive joy in living, and to contribute to the economic and social life of the community (Canadian Association of Occupational Therapy, 1997). Occupation is the goal of occupational therapy and the means by which we seek to modify a person's body functions (motor-sensory, perceptual-cognitive, and emotional-relational abilities). Generally, there are 3 areas in which we can find occupations: personal care, work (school), and free time. Occupational therapy is practiced in a wide range of settings, including hospitals, health centers, the home, workplaces, schools, and retirement homes (World Federation of Occupational Therapy). Occupational therapists adopt a person-centered approach and practice based on evidence (evidence-based health care).

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Mobility: Walking and Moving Around
content: Activities of Daily Living (ADL) Index: This is usually done through both interviews and observation. The observation component includes tasks such as toileting, personal grooming and hygiene, eating and drinking, dressing, and moving independently throughout the house. This is scored based on whether the patient can perform these tasks independently or requires assistance from another person.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Mobility: Walking and Moving Around
content: AM-PAC: AM-PAC stands for "Activity Measure for Post-Acute Care." The AM-PAC is an outcomes instrument that measures 3 domains: applied cognitive, basic mobility, and daily activities. This is often used to monitor and research outpatient rehabilitation, nursing home, and long-term acute care (LTAC) settings. [2]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Mobility: Walking and Moving Around
content: Modified Berthel Index: MBI is used to assess activities of daily living across 10 domains. These include bathing, feeding, stair climbing, personal hygiene, dressing, bowel control, bladder control, chair transfer, and ambulation. [3]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Mobility: Walking and Moving Around
content: Stroke Impact Scale: This self-reported questionnaire can evaluate patients' disability and quality of life after stroke.  It takes about 15 to 20 minutes to administer and requires no training. It covers 8 domains: memory and cognition, emotion, strength, communication, ADLs, mobility, hand function, and participation. Each item is scored from 1 to 5. A lower score signifies more ease in completing the task. [4]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Self Care
content: Melville-Nelson Self-Care Assessment This is a scale used by occupational therapists in subacute rehabilitation or skilled nursing facilities (SNFs). The interrater reliability was 94%. The 7 domains are bed mobility, transfers, dressing, eating, toileting, personal hygiene, and bathing. Each of these is divided into suboccupations. For instance, personal hygiene may be divided into hair brushing, handwashing, dental care, and even self-care. Those are then divided into sub-suboccupations. Dental hygiene may be subdivided into the right, left, upper, and lower arches. [7] occupations (bed mobility, transfers, dressing, eating, toileting, personal hygiene, bathing) are rated in 2 ways: self-performance (how much the person did) and support (the degree of assistance needed from others)

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Swallowing
content: The Mann Assessment of Swallowing Ability (MASA) This was first introduced to identify dysphagia in acute-stage stroke patients. It can now be used as a screening tool for any dependent older adult. [8] Acute Stroke Dysphagia Screen This is an easily administered and reliable tool that can be used to detect both dysphagia and aspiration risk in acute stroke patients. The interrater reliability is 93.6%, and the test-retest reliability was 92.5%. It also has a sensitivity>90% and a specificity>68% for detecting dysphagia and aspiration. Victorian Dysphagia Screening Model ASSIST Tool Completion of this is recommended by personnel who have completed approved dysphagia screening training. This is recommended in the presence of persistent acute stroke symptoms. Swallowing Ability and Function Evaluation  This test evaluates swallowing. Before this test is administered, a baseline evaluation of cognition and proper motor function should be assessed.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Attention
content: Test of Everyday Attention (TEA) The TEA is an attention test that provides an overview by breaking attention into distinct factors. This is achieved by including subtests, such as searching a telephone directory or listening to lottery results, that mimic everyday tasks. This is a useful assessment tool for work rehabilitation programs, particularly for jobs that require sustained attention, such as air traffic control. [9]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Attention
content: Neurobehavioral Cognitive Status Screening Examination (COGNISTAT) This assessment provides a brief screening of cognitive dysfunction. It provides profile scores for language constructions, memory, calculations, and reasoning. It also separately and independently assesses orientation, level of consciousness, and attention.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Attention
content: D2 Test of Attention This assessment is a cancellation test that can measure attention, visual scanning, and processing speed. It is a paper-and-pencil test that assesses whether the patient can focus attention on specific numbers, letters, and combinations of the 2 over a specified period. Cancellation test to measure attention, visual scanning, and processing speed. [10]

The domains assessed include memory capacity, strategy of use, and recall. Rivermead Behavioral Memory Test This assessment identifies everyday problems and is good at tracking change over time. title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Carrying Objects
content: Action Research Arm Test This test can assess limitations in upper-limb mobility following a brain insult. It should be used in people with a TBI (traumatic brain injury). [12] The scores from 19 specific tests are summed. These 19 specifics are spread along 4 specific subsets (grasp, grip, pincer, and gross movement). The 19 tests are given a number 0-3. 0 = no movement, 1 = the movement is partially performed, 2 = the movement is completed but takes a long time, and 3 = the movement is performed normally.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Carrying Objects
content: The Arm Motor Ability Test (AMAT) This is also a test to identify and assess upper extremity limitations quantitatively in patients who have had a stroke or any other insult to their brain. A study showed that a change of 0.44 or greater in the AMAT shows a clinically meaningful and statistically significant change. AMAT assesses functional ability, quality of movement, and performance time. [13]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Changing and Maintaining Body Position
content: Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS) This assessment takes time to administer. Those evaluated with AMPS are rated on 15 motor skills and 20 process skill items after being observed performing 2 or 3 IADLs. This provides an objective assessment of both motor and process skills. [14]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Changing and Maintaining Body Position
content: Berg Balance Scale This assessment, developed in 1989, was designed to identify and measure balance in older adults. It measures both static and dynamic abilities through functional tasks commonly performed in everyday life. The scale has 14 items, and each is scored on a scale of 0 to 4 with a total of 52 points. The higher the score, the better the balance. The interrater reliability is 97%. [15]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Issues of Concern -- Changing and Maintaining Body Position
content: Timed Get Up and Go Test The patient is observed and assessed as they rise from a chair, walk 3 meters, turn, walk back, and sit. The patient is timed during this test, and it has good interrater reliability. This aligns well with the previous Berg Balance Scale and can predict whether it would be safe for the patient to go outside. [16]

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Clinical Significance
content: The goal of rehabilitation, especially occupational therapy, is to help those return to the activities that they need and want to do. To this end, it is important to apply current research, evidence, and critical reasoning to achieve specific outcomes better. Formalized assessments are important because they reduce bias, which is essential for accurately classifying specific categories under assessment. These specific assessments listed above are important because they serve as a way to identify any deviations from 'normal.' These deviations can then be analyzed, and specific therapies can be used to address the patient/client's needs. Finally, the assessments provide a means to measure change over time and to track the progress the patient/client has made.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Clinical Significance
content: Occupational therapists work with individuals of all ages, from children to the elderly. The first appointment with an occupational therapist typically involves an assessment of the situation. This includes the history of any condition the patient has had and, in particular, an evaluation of the difference between what could be done in the past and what can be done now. Goal setting is an important part of occupational therapy. The occupational therapist works with the patient to determine which activities are most important to him and to establish clear goals to improve his ability to perform them. What often distinguishes occupational therapy from physiotherapy is that, while a physical therapist focuses on improving physical function and movement, an occupational therapist seeks to determine whether there is an alternative way to perform a given activity. Occupational therapy is, therefore, more oriented toward adaptation.

title: Occupational Therapy Assessment In Long Term Care -- Clinical Significance
content: Another important distinction between physiotherapists and occupational therapists is that the former work with patients in both acute and chronic phases, whereas the latter work with patients with chronic or resolving conditions.
